title: Pride and Prejudice
author: Jane Austen
premise: In a Hertfordshire village, Mrs. Bennet has five unmarried daughters and one mission. When a wealthy young bachelor rents the estate nearby, bringing along a proud and aloof friend, Elizabeth Bennet, the sharpest of the sisters, forms her opinions quickly. A comedy of manners about first impressions, and how wrong they can be.
pace: Quick and witty from the first page; much of it is conversation.

title: Moby-Dick
author: Herman Melville
premise: A restless young man signs on to a whaling ship out of Nantucket and discovers that its captain is hunting something far more personal than oil. Part sea adventure, part encyclopedia of whaling, part philosophical sermon: the great American novel about obsession.
pace: The story moves briskly at first, then regularly pauses for whole chapters on whales and whaling. Some readers love the detours, others skim them; both are fine.

title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
premise: A young scientist, consumed by the ambition to discover the secret of life, succeeds, and recoils from what he has made. Framed by the letters of an explorer sailing toward the North Pole, the novel Shelley began at eighteen asks what we owe to the things we create.
pace: Opens with a few letters from an Arctic explorer before the main story begins. They're short, and they matter.

title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
premise: Nick Carraway rents a small house on Long Island next to the mansion of Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire famous for his extravagant parties. Over one Jazz Age summer, Nick is drawn into the lives of the rich and restless around him. A short, luminous novel about longing and reinvention.
pace: Short and fast. Many readers finish it in two or three sittings.

title: Mrs Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
premise: One June day in London, 1923. Clarissa Dalloway walks through the city to buy flowers for the party she is giving that evening. Woolf follows her thoughts, and those of the people around her, as they move freely between the present and memory: a whole life seen through a single day.
pace: No chapters, and the point of view drifts from one person to another mid-paragraph. It takes a few pages to get used to, then it carries you.

title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
premise: In a provincial English town around 1830, the idealistic Dorothea Brooke longs to do something great with her life, while a young doctor arrives with plans to reform medicine. Eliot weaves their lives into a portrait of an entire community. Often called the greatest novel in English.
pace: Long and unhurried, with several stories woven together. It starts gently and deepens as the threads begin to cross.

title: Dom Casmurro
author: Machado de Assis
premise: An older man living alone in Rio de Janeiro decides to write his memoirs, to tie together the two ends of his life: his childhood, his first love for Capitu, the girl next door, and what became of them. The narrator is charming, digressive, and not necessarily to be trusted.
pace: Very short chapters, some only a paragraph long, and a narrator who talks to you directly. The 1899 spelling takes a page or two to get used to.

title: Memórias Póstumas de Brás Cubas
author: Machado de Assis
premise: Brás Cubas is dead, and finally free to be honest about his life. Writing from beyond the grave in short, playful, irreverent chapters, a wealthy Rio gentleman recounts his loves, ambitions and failures. The novel that changed Brazilian literature.
pace: Short, playful chapters, and the narrator constantly interrupts himself to talk to you. The 1881 spelling takes a page or two to get used to.

title: The Lady with the Dog
author: Anton Chekhov
premise: At the seaside resort of Yalta, a bored, married Moscow banker notices a young woman who walks alone every day with her small white dog. Chekhov's most famous story, and one of the great short stories about love.

title: The Student
author: Anton Chekhov
premise: On a cold Good Friday evening, a hungry seminary student walks home through the countryside and stops at a fire where two widows are warming themselves. A four-page story, often said to have been Chekhov's own favourite.

title: Gooseberries
author: Anton Chekhov
premise: Two friends caught in the rain take shelter at a country estate. One of them tells the story of his brother, a clerk who saved all his life for a little farm with a gooseberry bush. A story about happiness, and who pays for it.

title: Persuasion
author: Jane Austen
premise: Eight years ago, Anne Elliot was persuaded to break off her engagement to a young naval officer with no fortune. Now he is back, rich and admired, and she is twenty-seven, overlooked by her vain family. Austen's last completed novel, and her most quietly emotional.
pace: Shorter and quieter than Pride and Prejudice. The first chapters introduce a family before the story proper begins.

title: Jane Eyre
author: Charlotte Brontë
premise: An orphan raised by a cruel aunt grows up plain, poor, and fiercely independent, and takes a post as governess at a remote country house whose master is moody and whose upper floors hold a secret. Told in Jane's own unforgettable voice.
pace: Gripping from the start. The childhood chapters are short and intense.

title: Wuthering Heights
author: Emily Brontë
premise: A gentleman renting a house on the Yorkshire moors meets his strange landlord, Heathcliff, and asks the housekeeper for the story behind him. What she tells is a tale of two families and a passion that refuses to stay buried. Brontë's only novel.
pace: The first chapters are deliberately puzzling: a newcomer who doesn't understand what he's seeing. Things come into focus once the housekeeper starts telling the story.

title: Great Expectations
author: Charles Dickens
premise: Pip, an orphan raised by his harsh sister and her gentle blacksmith husband, has two chance encounters, one with an escaped convict and one with a strange rich woman in a decaying house, that change the course of his life. A novel about ambition, gratitude and snobbery.
pace: Opens with one of Dickens's most famous scenes. It was first published in weekly instalments, so chapters are short and often end on a hook.

title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
premise: In imperial Russian society, two stories unfold side by side: a married woman who falls into a passion that society will not forgive, and an awkward landowner searching for meaning in love, work and faith. Often called the greatest novel ever written.
pace: Long, but very readable: the chapters are short, and the book alternates between two main stories.

title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
premise: In the stifling summer heat of St. Petersburg, a penniless former student convinces himself that some people stand above ordinary morality, and resolves to prove it. A psychological thriller written from inside a feverish mind.
pace: Intense and feverish from the first page. The long, rambling monologues are part of the experience.

title: Song of Myself
author: Walt Whitman
premise: Whitman's great long poem: a celebration of the self, the body, the grass and the crowd, in which the 'I' who speaks keeps expanding to include everyone.
pace: Long and loose. You can read a single section and stop, or read straight through.

title: Crossing Brooklyn Ferry
author: Walt Whitman
premise: Standing on the ferry between Manhattan and Brooklyn at sunset, Whitman speaks directly to the people who will make the same crossing long after he is gone, which means to you.

title: Ode to a Nightingale
author: John Keats
premise: Listening to a nightingale on a spring night, the poet longs to escape with it from a world of sickness and time. Written in 1819, when Keats was twenty-three.

title: To Autumn
author: John Keats
premise: Keats's last great poem: three stanzas that move through the season from ripeness, to harvest, to the music of the year's end.

title: Ode on a Grecian Urn
author: John Keats
premise: The poet contemplates the scenes painted on an ancient Greek vase: lovers, musicians, a village procession, all frozen forever in a single moment.

title: Sonnet 18
author: William Shakespeare
premise: Shakespeare's most famous sonnet: fourteen lines that set out to compare someone to a summer's day and end up making a bold claim about what poetry can do.

title: Sonnet 29
author: William Shakespeare
premise: A sonnet that begins in envy, self-pity and disgrace, and turns, in a single thought, into something else entirely.

title: Sonnet 73
author: William Shakespeare
premise: An aging speaker describes himself through three images of ending: late autumn, twilight, a dying fire. Then he turns to the person he's speaking to.

title: Sonnet 116
author: William Shakespeare
premise: Shakespeare's definition of love that lasts, read at countless weddings, and sterner than its reputation.

title: Sonnet 130
author: William Shakespeare
premise: A love poem that refuses every cliché of love poetry: no eyes like the sun, no lips like coral. It's funny, and then it isn't.

title: Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening
author: Robert Frost
premise: A traveller pauses at dusk on the darkest evening of the year to watch snow fill a stranger's woods. Sixteen lines, and some of the best-known in American poetry.

title: Fire and Ice
author: Robert Frost
premise: Nine lines on how the world will end, written with a shrug that makes them more chilling.

title: Nothing Gold Can Stay
author: Robert Frost
premise: Eight lines about the first green of spring, and everything else that doesn't last.

title: Mending Wall
author: Robert Frost
premise: Two neighbours walk their shared stone wall each spring to repair it. One of them wonders why they bother.

title: The Lake Isle of Innisfree
author: W. B. Yeats
premise: Standing on a grey city pavement, the poet dreams of a small island in a lake in the west of Ireland. Yeats wrote it when he was homesick in London.

title: When You Are Old
author: W. B. Yeats
premise: A love poem addressed to a woman in her old age, asking her to remember the one person who loved her truly.

title: The Song of Wandering Aengus
author: W. B. Yeats
premise: A man goes fishing at night, catches a silver trout, and sees it turn into a girl who calls his name and vanishes. He spends his life looking for her.

title: He Wishes for the Cloths of Heaven
author: W. B. Yeats
premise: Eight lines from a poor man to the woman he loves. One of the shortest love poems in English, and one of the most quoted.

title: The Second Coming
author: W. B. Yeats
premise: Written just after the First World War, a vision of a world coming apart, and of something new and terrible on its way.

title: The Negro Speaks of Rivers
author: Langston Hughes
premise: Written when Hughes was seventeen, crossing the Mississippi by train: a poem that traces a people's memory through the great rivers of history.

title: Mother to Son
author: Langston Hughes
premise: A mother tells her son that life for her "ain't been no crystal stair", and tells him not to stop climbing.

title: Dreams
author: Langston Hughes
premise: Eight lines on why dreams are worth holding on to. Short enough to memorize, and many people have.

title: I, Too
author: Langston Hughes
premise: A Black man sent to eat in the kitchen when company comes, and his quiet certainty about tomorrow. An answer to Whitman's "I Hear America Singing".

title: The Weary Blues
author: Langston Hughes
premise: A night in Harlem: the poet listens to a piano player sing the blues, and the poem itself starts to move like the music.

title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
author: T. S. Eliot
premise: A timid, aging man walks through a foggy city on his way to a tea party, rehearsing a question he may never dare to ask. The poem that announced modern poetry.

title: Preludes
author: T. S. Eliot
premise: Four short scenes of a city from evening to morning: smoke, rain, cheap rooms, and the lives inside them.

title: The Raven
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: At midnight in December, a grieving student hears a tapping at his door. What comes in is a raven that knows a single word.

title: Annabel Lee
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: Poe's last complete poem: a love story from a "kingdom by the sea", told with the rhythm of a ballad.

title: Alone
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: Written when Poe was twenty and unpublished until after his death: a young man explaining why he has always felt different from everyone else.

title: Dulce et Decorum Est
author: Wilfred Owen
premise: Written in the trenches of the First World War by a soldier who didn't survive it: a gas attack, and an answer to everyone who called dying for your country sweet.

title: Anthem for Doomed Youth
author: Wilfred Owen
premise: A sonnet asking what funeral rites there are for soldiers who "die as cattle". Owen drafted it in hospital with Siegfried Sassoon's help.

title: Gitanjali 35
author: Rabindranath Tagore
premise: From the collection that made Tagore the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature: a prayer for a free country, written in his own English translation.

title: Success is counted sweetest
author: Emily Dickinson
premise: Twelve lines arguing that only people who fail truly understand what success means.

title: There's a certain slant of light
author: Emily Dickinson
premise: A winter afternoon, a particular light, and the strange despair it brings. Dickinson at her most precise about feelings nobody else names.

title: Because I could not stop for Death
author: Emily Dickinson
premise: Death arrives as a polite gentleman caller and takes the speaker for a slow carriage ride.

title: I'm nobody! Who are you?
author: Emily Dickinson
premise: Eight playful lines in praise of being nobody, from a poet who published almost nothing in her lifetime.

title: Hope is the thing with feathers
author: Emily Dickinson
premise: Hope as a small bird that lives inside you and sings, whatever the weather.

title: I heard a fly buzz when I died
author: Emily Dickinson
premise: A deathbed scene, told by the person dying, and interrupted by a fly.

title: The Cask of Amontillado
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: During carnival in an Italian city, a man who has been insulted invites the insulter down to his wine cellars to taste a rare sherry. A short tale of revenge, told by the one taking it.

title: The Fall of the House of Usher
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A man rides to the crumbling mansion of a childhood friend who has written begging for company. The friend, the house and his sister are all, in different ways, unwell.

title: The Masque of the Red Death
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: While a plague ravages the country, a prince shuts himself and a thousand courtiers inside a fortified abbey and throws a masked ball.

title: Araby
author: James Joyce
premise: A Dublin boy is in love with his friend's older sister, and promises to bring her something from a bazaar called Araby.

title: Eveline
author: James Joyce
premise: A young woman in Dublin sits by the window on the evening she has promised to leave home for good.

title: The Dead
author: James Joyce
premise: Two elderly sisters throw their annual Christmas party in Dublin, and their nephew Gabriel frets about the speech he has to give. Often called the greatest short story in English.

title: The Story of an Hour
author: Kate Chopin
premise: A woman with a weak heart is gently given terrible news. What follows, alone in her room, takes about an hour. (First published as "The Dream of an Hour".)

title: The Gift of the Magi
author: O. Henry
premise: It's Christmas Eve, and a young New York wife has one dollar and eighty-seven cents to buy her husband a present.

title: Hills Like White Elephants
author: Ernest Hemingway
premise: An American and a young woman wait for a train at a station in Spain, drinking and talking about something they never name.

title: Cat in the Rain
author: Ernest Hemingway
premise: In a hotel in Italy, an American wife sees a cat sheltering from the rain under a table outside and wants it.

title: To the Lighthouse
author: Virginia Woolf
premise: The Ramsay family and their guests spend a summer at their house on a Scottish island, where a small boy longs to sail to the lighthouse across the bay. Woolf follows the thoughts of everyone in the house, and what time does to them.
pace: There's very little plot, and a lot happens inside people's heads. Read it slowly, like a long poem; the middle section is short and strange.

title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
author: Oscar Wilde
premise: A beautiful young man sits for his portrait and, under the influence of a witty, cynical lord, makes a wish: that the painting would grow old instead of him.
pace: Starts with a famous preface of one-line provocations, then long, glittering conversations. Wilde's dialogue is half the pleasure.

title: The Bet
author: Anton Chekhov
premise: At a party, a rich banker and a young lawyer argue about whether death is kinder than life in prison. They settle it with a wager: two million roubles if the young man can stay locked in a garden lodge, alone, for fifteen years.
pace: Short, and quick to the end. Most of the story is the years in the lodge, told briskly.

title: Misery
author: Anton Chekhov
premise: On a snowy evening in St Petersburg, an old sledge-driver picks up fare after fare. He has something he needs to tell someone, and nobody will listen.
pace: Very short and quiet; you can read it in ten minutes.

title: A Little Cloud
author: James Joyce
premise: Little Chandler, a shy Dublin clerk who dreams of being a poet, goes to meet an old friend who left for London and made it as a journalist. Over whiskey, the friend talks, and Chandler compares lives.
pace: Mostly one long conversation in a bar, then a short scene at home.

title: A Painful Case
author: James Joyce
premise: Mr Duffy, a Dublin bank cashier, lives alone by strict and careful habits. At a concert he falls into conversation with a married woman, and for the first time someone shares his evenings.
pace: Short and spare; Joyce at his most exact.

title: Désirée’s Baby
author: Kate Chopin
premise: In old Louisiana, a girl found as a toddler by the gate of a plantation grows up and marries the proud son of a neighbouring family. Then she has a baby, and something changes in the house.
pace: Very short. Read it in one sitting, all the way to the last line.

title: The Last Leaf
author: O. Henry
premise: Two young women artists share a studio in Greenwich Village. When one falls ill with pneumonia, she starts counting the leaves on the ivy outside her window.
pace: Short and warm, with O. Henry's usual jokes and a famous ending.

title: The Ransom of Red Chief
author: O. Henry
premise: Two small-time crooks in Alabama kidnap the son of a rich man and hide him in a cave, planning to ask two thousand dollars. They have not met the boy yet.
pace: A comic story told by one of the crooks, quick and very funny.

title: The Oval Portrait
author: Edgar Allan Poe
premise: A wounded traveller spends the night in an abandoned château in the Apennines. By candlelight he notices a portrait of a young woman, and finds a book that tells its story.
pace: Poe's shortest tale: two pages, a story within a story.

title: In Another Country
author: Ernest Hemingway
premise: Milan, during the First World War. A young American, recovering from a wound, spends his afternoons at a hospital on machines meant to repair the body, beside an Italian major who was once a champion fencer.
pace: Short, plain sentences; a lot is left unsaid.

title: Soldier’s Home
author: Ernest Hemingway
premise: Harold Krebs comes home to Oklahoma from the war long after the parades are over. He sleeps late, reads, and watches the girls in town, and his mother wants to know what he plans to do with his life.
pace: Short, with a long breakfast-table conversation at its heart.

title: Madame Bovary
author: Gustave Flaubert
premise: Emma, a farmer's daughter raised on romantic novels, marries Charles Bovary, a kind and dull country doctor, and moves to a small town in Normandy. Marriage is nothing like the books promised, and she starts looking for the life she read about.
pace: Slow and exact: Flaubert worked over every sentence, and the story builds quietly.

title: The Age of Innocence
author: Edith Wharton
premise: New York high society in the 1870s. Newland Archer, a young lawyer, is about to announce his engagement to May Welland, the ideal girl of his set, when her cousin Ellen comes home from Europe, after leaving her husband, a Polish count, and sets everyone talking.
pace: Elegant and ironic, with long, polished sentences. Most of the drama is in what people don't say.

title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
author: Mark Twain
premise: Huck Finn, a boy who'd rather sleep outdoors than be "sivilized", escapes his drunken father and heads down the Mississippi on a raft with Jim, a man escaping slavery. Told in Huck's own voice.
pace: Told in Huck's dialect, which takes a few pages to settle into. It uses the racial language of its time, including slurs.

title: The Awakening
author: Kate Chopin
premise: Edna Pontellier, a wife and mother from New Orleans, spends a summer at a resort on the Gulf of Mexico. Something in her begins to change, and she stops wanting to live the way she's expected to.
pace: Short for a novel and easy to read: short chapters, clear prose, a lot of sea.

title: Notes from Underground
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
premise: A bitter, brilliant former civil servant in St Petersburg, living alone, writes down everything that's wrong with himself and with the idea that people act in their own interest. Then he tells a story from his youth.
pace: The first part is a long, argumentative monologue; the second is a story and moves faster.
